title: Mind-Bending Maths · Episode 3
chapters: Nature's geometry: hexagons, spirals and bubbles
Benford's law: why so many numbers start with 1
Ramanujan: the clerk who wrote to Cambridge

units.t: Mind-Bending Maths. Episode three.
In this episode: Nature's geometry: hexagons, spirals and bubbles, Chaos and the butterfly effect, Benford's law: why so many numbers start with 1 and Ramanujan: the clerk who wrote to Cambridge.
Part one. Nature's geometry: hexagons, spirals and bubbles.
Bees build hexagons, sunflowers count in Fibonacci numbers and soap bubbles solve maths problems in an instant.
Nature is full of geometry, and there are good reasons why.
The bee's hexagon.
Honeycomb is made of near-perfect hexagons.
Only three regular shapes fit together on a flat surface with no gaps: triangles, squares and hexagons.
Of these, hexagons enclose a given area with the shortest total wall.
For cells of equal area, a square needs about 7.
5 per cent more perimeter than a hexagon, and a triangle about 22 per cent more.
Bees must eat honey to make wax, so saving wax saves energy.
Around 300 CE Pappus of Alexandria praised bees for their geometric wisdom.
The stronger claim, that hexagons beat every possible way of dividing a flat surface into equal areas, was only proved in 1999, by the mathematician Thomas Hales.
It is known as the honeycomb conjecture.
Sunflower spirals.
Look closely at a large sunflower and you will see seeds in two sets of spirals, one clockwise and one anticlockwise.
Count them and you often get neighbouring Fibonacci numbers, such as 34 and 55, or 55 and 89.
Pinecones, pineapples and daisy centres show smaller pairs, like 8 and 13.
The pattern is common rather than universal.
A large citizen science project published in 2016, inspired by Alan Turing's interest in sunflowers, counted the spirals on hundreds of seed heads.
A sizeable minority did not fit simple Fibonacci patterns.
Nature leans strongly towards these numbers, but it is not an unbreakable rule.
The golden angle.
A sunflower head grows from the centre, adding seeds one at a time, each at a fixed angle from the one before.
If that angle were a simple fraction of a turn, such as a quarter, seeds would line up in four straight spokes with big gaps between them.
The angle that best avoids lining up is about 137.
5 degrees, called the golden angle.
It is linked to the golden ratio, the number that resists approximation by simple fractions more than any other.
With it, seeds fill the head evenly and pack in as many as possible.
The spirals we see, and their Fibonacci counts, are a side effect of that efficient packing, and computer models reproduce them from this one rule.
Bubbles solve problems.
Blow a single soap bubble and it becomes a sphere.
For any amount of air, a sphere has the smallest possible surface, and surface tension pulls the soap film as tight as it can go.
When bubbles cluster in a foam, they follow rules set out by the Belgian physicist Joseph Plateau in 1873.
Soap films always meet in threes, at equal angles of 120 degrees, and the edges where films meet always come together in fours, at about 109.
5 degrees.
Dip a wire frame into soapy water and the film often forms the smallest surface spanning it, instantly solving a problem that can take pages of calculation.
The architect Frei Otto used soap film models to design light, curving roofs.
Spirals, size and stone.
A snail or nautilus cannot remodel its shell, so it adds material at the open end and each turn is a scaled-up copy of the last.
The result is close to a logarithmic spiral, which keeps its shape however far you zoom.
Jacob Bernoulli called it the 'marvellous spiral' and asked for it on his gravestone, though the mason carved the wrong kind.
Claims that the nautilus follows the golden ratio do not survive careful measurement.
Geometry also limits size.
Double an ant's length, width and height and its leg strength rises four times, but its weight rises eight.
Galileo described this square-cube law in 1638, which is why elephants have stout legs.
Slowly cooling lava cracks at angles near 120 degrees into columns, as at the Giant's Causeway and Organ Pipes National Park near Melbourne.
The key idea: Hexagons enclose a given area with the least wall, so bees save wax by building them.
Part two. Chaos and the butterfly effect.
A weather scientist rounded off a number and went to get a coffee.
When he came back, he had discovered why the future can never be fully predicted.
The clockwork universe.
After Isaac Newton showed that simple laws could explain the motions of the planets, the universe began to look like a precise machine.
In 1814, the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace described an imaginary intellect that knew the position of every particle and every force acting on them.
For such a being, he wrote, nothing would be uncertain, and the future would be as clear as the past.
Later writers called it Laplace's demon.
The idea was not foolish.
Astronomers could predict eclipses centuries ahead.
It seemed that the only obstacle to predicting anything, including the weather, was gathering enough data and doing enough calculation.
Poincaré's error.
In the 1880s, King Oscar II of Sweden offered a prize for proof that the solar system was stable in the long run.
The French mathematician Henri Poincaré studied a simplified version, three bodies moving under each other's gravity, and won in 1889.
Then, as his paper was being prepared for publication, a serious error was found.
Correcting it, Poincaré realised the three-body problem could behave in extraordinarily tangled ways, with tiny changes leading to vastly different orbits.
The printed copies had to be recalled and destroyed, reportedly at a cost greater than the prize money.
His corrected work is now seen as an early glimpse of chaos theory.
Lorenz's coffee break.
Edward Lorenz was a meteorologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who had built a simple weather model on an early computer.
In 1961, wanting to look at one run more closely, he restarted it partway through, typing in numbers from an earlier printout.
The printout had rounded to three decimal places, so instead of 0.
506127 he entered 0.
The difference was about one part in four thousand.
He went for a coffee while the slow machine worked.
When he returned, the new forecast had tracked the old one for a while, then drifted further and further away until the two bore no resemblance.
Lorenz realised this was not a computer fault.
It was a property of the weather.
The butterfly effect.
Lorenz published in 1963, but his work reached a wide audience after a 1972 talk.
Its title, reportedly suggested by a colleague, asked: ‘Does the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?’
It was a question, not a claim that butterflies control the weather.
By coincidence, a plot of his equations looks like a pair of butterfly wings.
A chaotic system is deterministic: the same start always gives the same result, with no randomness in the rules.
The catch is sensitive dependence on initial conditions.
Tiny differences grow, roughly doubling again and again, until they swamp everything.
Since we can never measure perfectly, predictions eventually fail.
Release a double pendulum twice from what looks like the same position and the swings soon diverge wildly.
Living with chaos.
Chaos explains why weather forecasts are reliable for a few days, useful for about a week, and of little value beyond about two weeks.
Forecasters deal with this honestly through ensembles, running a model many times with slightly different starting conditions.
If the runs agree, confidence is high; if they spread out, the outlook is uncertain.
Chaos turns up elsewhere too.
In 1976, the Australian-born scientist Robert May showed that a very simple equation for animal populations could swing from steady numbers to wild booms and busts.
Even planetary orbits are thought to be chaotic over tens of millions of years.
Laplace's demon would need infinitely precise data, and nature never provides that.
The key idea: After Newton, many scientists believed that perfect knowledge of the present would allow perfect prediction of the future.
Part three. Benford's law: why so many numbers start with 1.
In many tables of real-world numbers, from river areas to company accounts, almost a third begin with the digit 1.
The pattern is real, it can be explained, and it has helped auditors spot cooked books.
Worn pages, odd pattern.
Before calculators, scientists looked up logarithms in thick books of tables.
In 1881 the astronomer Simon Newcomb noticed that the early pages, covering numbers starting with 1, were far more worn than the later ones.
People were looking up numbers beginning with 1 much more often than those beginning with 9.
His short note was largely forgotten.
In 1938 the physicist Frank Benford, working at General Electric, noticed the same thing independently.
He collected more than 20,000 numbers from around 20 very different sources, including river areas, city populations, physical constants and magazine figures.
The same lopsided pattern appeared again and again, and it now carries his name.
The lopsided pattern.
You might expect each leading digit, 1 to 9, to turn up about 11 per cent of the time.
In data that follow Benford's law, they don't.
About 30.
1 per cent of numbers start with 1.
Around 17.
6 per cent start with 2, 12.
5 per cent with 3 and 9.
7 per cent with 4.
The share keeps falling: 7.
9 per cent for 5, 6.
8 for 7 and 5.
1 for 8, down to just 4.
6 per cent for 9.
The formula uses logarithms: the chance of a leading digit d is the base 10 logarithm of one plus one divided by d.
Why growth favours 1.
Imagine a town of 100 people growing by 10 per cent a year.
Doubling to 200 takes a little over seven years, all spent starting with a 1.
Going from 200 to 300 takes a little over four.
Going from 900 to 1,000, a rise of just 11 per cent, takes about a year, and then it must double again to escape the 1s.
Populations, prices, investments and revenues grow by multiplying, so they linger on low leading digits.
The pattern also holds in any units: convert dollars to yen, or kilometres to miles, and it stays the same.
In 1961 Roger Pinkham showed that any law of leading digits independent of units would have to be Benford's law.
When it doesn't apply.
Benford's law is not a law of nature that every list must obey.
It works best for numbers that spread across several orders of magnitude, say from tens to tens of thousands, and that arise from natural processes or from combining other numbers.
It fails for data stuck in a narrow range.
Adult heights in centimetres almost all start with 1, because nearly everyone is between 100 and 199 centimetres tall.
It also fails for numbers that people assign, such as phone numbers, postcodes and lottery numbers, and for prices deliberately set at points like $9.
Before applying the law to any data set, ask whether there is a good reason to expect it to fit at all.
Catching cooked books.
People who invent numbers tend to spread first digits fairly evenly, because that feels random.
Real financial data, such as invoices, often follow Benford's law closely, so the gap is a useful screening tool.
Mark Nigrini helped popularise it in auditing in the 1990s.
A deviation does not prove fraud and often has an innocent explanation, such as many identical fees.
It is also easy to misuse.
After the 2020 US election, online posts claimed some vote counts broke the law and proved fraud.
Statisticians replied that precinct totals cluster in a narrow range, so no fit was expected.
Always ask whether the data should fit the pattern first.
The key idea: Benford's law was spotted twice, first in worn logarithm books and later in thousands of real-world numbers.
Part four. Ramanujan: the clerk who wrote to Cambridge.
A largely self-taught clerk in Madras posted pages of strange formulas to a famous English mathematician.
They were so astonishing that they changed both men's lives.
A borrowed book.
Srinivasa Ramanujan was born on 22 December 1887 in Erode, in southern India, and grew up in Kumbakonam.
As a teenager he found a book by George Shoobridge Carr, a summary of several thousand mathematical results, mostly given without proofs.
He worked through it alone, filling notebooks with his own discoveries.
His obsession had a cost.
He won a college scholarship but neglected his other subjects, failed his exams and lost it.
For several years he lived in poverty, working with little guidance.
Eventually supporters who recognised his talent helped him find a job as a clerk at the Madras Port Trust in 1912, giving him a small wage and time to keep working.
The letter to Cambridge.
In January 1913 Ramanujan wrote to Godfrey Harold Hardy, a leading mathematician at Trinity College, Cambridge, enclosing pages of formulas, many about infinite series, without proof.
Hardy got many letters from cranks and was tempted to dismiss it.
But he and John Littlewood realised the pages were remarkable: some results known, a few wrong, many new and astonishing.
Hardy said some must be true, because no one would have had the imagination to invent them otherwise.
Ramanujan sailed for England in 1914.
Hardy insisted on rigorous proofs, while Ramanujan reached results by intuition, saying some came from his family goddess Namagiri.
Wartime Cambridge was hard for a strict vegetarian far from home, yet in 1918 he became a Fellow of the Royal Society, one of the first Indians so honoured.
The taxicab number.
The most famous story comes from Hardy.
Visiting his friend in hospital, Hardy remarked that he had arrived in taxi number 1729, which seemed a rather dull number.
Ramanujan replied that, on the contrary, it was very interesting.
It is the smallest number that can be written as the sum of two cubes in two different ways.
Check it: 1 cubed plus 12 cubed is 1 plus 1,728, which is 1,729.
And 9 cubed plus 10 cubed is 729 plus 1,000, which is also 1,729.
Numbers with this property are now called taxicab numbers.
The story captures something real about Ramanujan, who knew individual numbers like old friends.
Breaking numbers into pieces.
One of their greatest achievements concerns partitions, the ways to write a whole number as a sum of positive whole numbers.
The number 4 has five: 4, 3 plus 1, 2 plus 2, 2 plus 1+1 and 1 plus 1+1 plus 1.
Counts explode as numbers grow.
The number 200 has 3,972,999,029,388, a figure Percy MacMahon worked out painstakingly by hand.
Hardy and Ramanujan found a formula that estimated such values with astonishing accuracy, later refined into an exact formula.
Ramanujan also spotted hidden patterns.
The partition counts of 4, 9, 14, 19, 24 and so on, every fifth number, are always divisible by 5.
Those counts begin 5, 30, 135, 490 and 1,575.
A short life, long legacy.
By 1917 Ramanujan was seriously ill.
The cause is still debated; tuberculosis and a liver infection, amoebiasis, have both been suggested.
He returned to India in 1919, still working on ‘mock theta functions’, and died on 26 April 1920, aged 32.
In 1976 George Andrews found a bundle of later papers, the ‘lost notebook’, in Trinity's library.
Researchers spent decades proving its results, and some ideas have found uses in modern physics.
His 1914 formulas for pi later helped computers calculate millions of digits.
India celebrates 22 December as National Mathematics Day.
His story is also a warning: he was found partly by luck, through supporters and one letter that reached the right reader.
Hardy wondered how much more he might have achieved with an earlier, fuller education.
The key idea: Ramanujan taught himself mathematics from a book of results with few proofs, at the cost of his formal education.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why do bees build hexagonal cells?
Answer. They need the least wall, which saves wax.
Question two. What did Laplace's imaginary intellect illustrate?
Answer. Perfect data would make the future knowable.
Question three. What did the worn pages in the logarithm books suggest?
Answer. Numbers starting with 1 were looked up far more often.
Question four. What did Ramanujan's obsession with mathematics cost him?
Answer. His formal education.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
